title: Superexchange coupling between a dilute Gd3+ probe and orphan spins in a valence-bond glass
authors: Patrick Colgan, Artur Solodovnyk, Jeremy P. Carlo, Scott Dietrich
abstract: The valence-bond-glass state of the 4d^1 double perovskite Ba2YMoO6 combines Mo^5+ singlets with residual paramagnetic "orphan" spins whose coupling is hard to reach with bulk probes. We probe them by electron paramagnetic resonance of a dilute Gd^3+ ion on the Y^3+ site via broadband coplanar-waveguide transmission at 5 K. The isostructural nonmagnetic niobate Ba2YNbO6, doped with the same Gd^3+ probe, is a fixed-lattice control. The Gd^3+ linewidth nearly doubles in the magnetic host. Dipolar coupling to the sparse orphans is nearly an order of magnitude too weak; the excess is instead reproduced by a transferred f-d superexchange of J ~ 0.2 K, so the width is a static measure of orphan-spin coupling. The half-field (Delta m_S = +/-2) satellite collapses in the magnetic host, a dynamical dephasing channel, while the unchanged g-factor marks a zero-mean random internal field. Together the two channels probe the coupling and dynamics of valence-bond-glass orphan spins.
summary: This experimental work uses Electron Paramagnetic Resonance on a dilute $	ext{Gd}^{3+}$ probe to investigate the magnetic coupling within a valence-bond-glass material. By analyzing both the static linewidth and the dynamic collapse of a satellite transition, the authors successfully attribute the coupling to a superexchange interaction rather than simple dipolar coupling. This provides a detailed, site-specific picture of the magnetic dynamics in these complex correlated materials.
main_problem: The study aims to characterize the magnetic coupling and dynamics of elusive 'orphan' spins residing within a valence-bond-glass state.
main_result: The excess linewidth in the magnetic host is determined to arise from a transferred f-d superexchange coupling ($J \approx 0.2 	ext{ K}$), while the half-field satellite collapse probes the dynamic dephasing of these orphan moments.
method: Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) spectroscopy using broadband coplanar-waveguide transmission is employed to probe the dilute $	ext{Gd}^{3+}$ probe spin.
model_or_system: The system is the double perovskite $	ext{Ba}_2	ext{YMoO}_6$, which exhibits a valence-bond-glass state containing residual paramagnetic 'orphan' spins. The measurement is compared against the isostructural, nonmagnetic control $	ext{Ba}_2	ext{YNbO}_6$.
key_observables: Linewidth (static coupling measure), half-field satellite collapse (dynamic dephasing channel), and the $	ext{g}$-factor.
important_parameters: The coupling strength $J \approx 0.2 	ext{ K}$; the temperature is fixed at $5 	ext{ K}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the $	ext{g}$-factor remains constant and that the observed half-field collapse is due to dynamical dephasing.
figures_summary: Figures show structural confirmations (XRD) and 2D maps of the $	ext{S}_{21}$ signal, illustrating the resonance features for both the main line and the half-field satellite in the $	ext{Mo}$ and $	ext{Nb}$ hosts.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the $	ext{Mo}$ (magnetic) and $	ext{Nb}$ (nonmagnetic) hosts using EPR. It first rules out simple dipolar coupling, then quantifies the excess width via the static linewidth, and finally analyzes the half-field satellite collapse to characterize the dynamic coupling mechanisms.
why_interesting: The use of EPR to distinguish between static (linewidth) and dynamic (satellite collapse) coupling channels in a complex magnetic state provides a powerful, site-resolved spectroscopic tool for understanding glassy magnetism.

Figure 3 shows representative field-swept absorption spectra ∆|S21|(B) for the Nb and Mo hosts at three fre- quencies, together with the two-Dysonian fits. Each spec- trum is well described by a main Gd3+ resonance and a weaker half-field satellite on a smooth non-resonant back- ground, with comparable fit quality across the resolved frequency range and for both hosts. At fixed frequency the Mo-host resonance is visibly broader than that of the Nb host.
